Telephonic Counselling Services
NACO has set up a National AIDS Help line on a toll free number 1097.   Callers can avail of counseling services round
the clock on this number.   The telephone is linked to a computerized voice response system which gives information on various
issues related to HIV/AIDS such as the general information on HIV/AIDS, symptoms of HIV infection/AIDS, testing of HIV
and care and support services for those infected and affected by HIV/AIDS.   Interested callers can also avail of personal
counselling.
            These services are very  useful since they maintain the confidentiality of the caller.
Such services have already been successfully implemented in Delhi, Calcutta, Hyderabad, Chandigarh, Guwahati,
Chennai and Patna.
Counselling Services in Government Hospitals
A model HIV councelling center has been set up at the Department of Skin and STD, Safdajung Hospital.  The project is
a joint collaboration of NACO, STD Department of Safdarjung Hospital and six Delhi based NGOs.   The counselling center,
the first of its kind to be set up in a government hospital, has the following objective:
Counselling Services in Voluntary Testing Centres
Voluntary testing Centres have been set up in all Government hospitals.   It would be mandatory to have pre and post
test counseling in these centers.   The counseling services would be provided by a trained NGO.         
Further Comments    

NINETY-NINTH REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/99threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:13:15]
When asked by the Committee , whether the Department is taking any step to open such model counseling centers in
different parts of the country,     the Department replied that it is proposed to set up voluntary testing and counseling centers in
all the district hospitals in the country on the basis of the model counseling center at Safdarjung Hospital, Delhi.  These
voluntary testing and counseling centers would be run by qualified and trained NGOs and would be funded by the concerned
State/UT/Corporation AIDS Control Societies.   Protocols and guidelines are also being  formulated for such centers.
Recommendation
3.8               The Committee is of the firm view that much emphasis under the AIDS control programme has not been so far laid on
the high risk behaviour groups like sex workers and frequently travelling males and drug users.   These are main groups which
are highly vulnerable to HIV/AIDS infection.   Awareness and counseling are much more required on these people than on the
other group of the society.   They should be made to understand the danger of the STD/HIV/AIDS and the risk factor involved
in not using condoms and taking other precautions.  Special awareness programme should be taken up particularly for sex
workers and frequently travelling males.
Reply of Government
3.8               NACO is implementing targeted intervention programmes to prevent the spread of infection in the high risk
marginalized population.   A multi pronged approach has been devised to contain further transmission of HIV within this group
or to other strata of society through them, as also to give health care and support services to those already infected.   A
combination of IEC strategies, including counselling, and relevant service provision, such as STD care and condoms, can be
used to create an enabling environment for people to scrutinize their behaviour and effect a change to protect themselves.
NACO is working with donor agencies in cooperation with the State Governments to conduct pilot programmes with
identified groups using an integrated approach.  Examples of successful targeted intervention programmes include Sonagachi
intervention project in Calcutta, Kamathipura Intervention project in Bombay and Continuum of care project in Manipur.   In the
second phase of the AIDS control project these targetted intervention programmes would be scaled up to cover vulnerable
populations in all states.
Recommendation
3.10      The Committee has learnt that various international agencies are implementing various programmes in different parts of
the country for tackling the problem of HIV/AIDS.   In this connection the Committee is constrained to note that NACO is not
involved in the implementation of all the projects in all parts of the country.  For example even though many pilot programmes
are being implemented in Tamil Nadu, NACO is involved with the implementation of only USAID Project.   The Committee
recommends that  NACO should be involved in the implementation of all pilot projects in all parts of the country so that it has
complete information about the implementation of all the projects.
Reply of Government
3.10      A steering committee has been formed in all the states where bilateral agencies are implementing intervention projects.  
These steering committees have a representative from NACO as well as the Project Director of the State AIDS Societies as
members.   The steering committee meets regularly and all decisions are taken in consultation with the representatives of the
Central and State Governments.
Recommendation
3.11      The  Committee is constrained to note that many states were performing very slow and the World Bank Mission in its
mid term review in 1995 recommended discontinuance of credit to such states.   The Committee was given to understand that
the reasons for slow performance were non-adherence to action plan, non-availability of infrastructure, political and social
problems.  It also appears that many states do not perceive the AIDS Control Programme as their own concern.   The
Empowered Committees of the States have also not been effective and have little control over initiating activities.   The
Committee perceives that there is still lack of awareness and enthusiasm in the states.   If the State Governments do not rise to
the occasion and pool in all the sources and energies available with them, it would be difficult to tackle the problems of
AIDS/HIV either by the Central Government or any international agency.   It is the State Governments which are nearer to the
people and which implement the programme.   They should therefore, be more concerned about the problem.   The Central
Government should, therefore, seriously consider this aspect.
 
Reply of Government
3.11            In order to develop ownership of the programme in States/UTs, State AIDS Societies have been constituted under the
Chairpersonship of Health Secretary.   The Society also includes representatives of NGOs as well as other related departments

NINETY-NINTH REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/99threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:13:15]
for effective coordination and implementation of the programme.   There is complete decentralization of the programme activity
to State level.   The role of the Central Government is only to provide technical expertise and policy guidelines.   The society
model will also ensure expeditious flow of funds from Central Government to programme implementation in the states.
Recommendation
3.12            The Committee was informed that efforts were being made to introduce AIDS education in the Schools.   It is true that
young people in India are equally vulnerable to HIV infection and they are also required to be educated in proper atmosphere.  
Inclusion of AIDS education as a part of the curriculum is of course one of the best alternatives to increase awareness about it.  
The Committee desires that it should be finalized as early as possible and it should be introduced from the academic year 1998-
99 onwards.
Reply of Government
3.12      Special programmes are being broadcast for the youth and rural/migrant populations on All India Radio FM and Vividh
Bharti respectively.   These programmes are in the entertainment mode with the objective of creating awareness and counseling
those who have specific queries or problems.   The programme on Vividh Bharti is broadcast in 11 regional languages.
A School AIDS Education Prograamme has been initiated to provide life skills education to high school students with a
component on HIV/AIDS.   The plan advocates a co-curricular approach in implementing School AIDS education.   It is
proposed to cover all the schools in a planned manner over the next five years.   The main components of the plan are advocacy
for opinion leaders, sensitization workshop for school principals, training of model teachers and peer education and school level
activities.
NACO  has also approached NCERT who have agreed to include information on HIV/AIDS in the curriculum.
Recommendation
3.14      The main concern facing the world community now is non-development of any vaccine for HIV/AIDS so far.   Many
countries are still in the process of research on this.   However, the Committee is constrained to note that no research on
development of vaccine for this has been initiated in India so far.   The Committee desires that our country also should
contribute its own mite, for it may so happen that the research conducted in India may ultimately lead to success.
Reply of Government
3.14      The Department of Biotechnology, Department of Science and Technology, All India Institute of Medical Sciences,
Delhi, National AIDS Research Institute, Pune and National Institute of Immunology, Delhi are involved in research in HIV
vaccine.   The Govt. of India encourages research in this field.
Recommendation
5.4         The Committee views with concern that mass awareness about Hepatitis B has not yet been taken up by the
Department.   People need to be educated about Hepatitis B virus the way it is being done in the case of HIV.   The IEC
activities in this regard need to be stepped up, and the Department should make use of all modes of IEC to spread the message
about Hepatitis B.   Special efforts need to be taken by the Department especially in the rural areas where people are still
unaware of it.  Steps should also be taken to print Pamphlets in the vernacular languages to address the issue among the rural
people.   NGOs can be successfully involved in this awareness campaign.
Reply of Government
5.4        Central Health Education Bureau, a subordinate office of the Directorate General of Health Services, Ministry of Health
and Family Welfare has undertaken a mass campaign to enlighten the public about the protection from viral Hepatitis (Jaundice)
by distribution of one lakh handbills to (1) State Health Education Bureau; (2)Directors of Health Services; (3) Department of
Prevention and Social Medicine (Medical Colleges); (4) Assistant Directors of Health Services; (5) National Medical Libraries;
(6) District Medical Offices; (7) Councils and Institute of India (Health); (8) Subscribers of Swasth Hind and Arogya Sandesh;
and (9) distributed to general public in the Family Welfare Pavilion during India International  Trade Fair 99. A press
advertisement on the subject was also given in the leading newspapers from 17th July to 3rd August, 1997 all over India.
Information, Education and Communication is an important component of the National AIDS Control Programme. 
Various communication media like electronic, print inter-personal communication and folk media etc. are being
intensively used for dissemination of information on HIV/AIDS.

IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT REPLIES
Recommendation
3.5               The Committee is aware that there is no cure for AIDS.  Prevention is the only aspect which has to be strengthened. 
For prevention a large scale public awareness is required.  The Committee is, however, constrained to note that the  awareness
programme has not picked up in India.  Even though the problem of AIDS is enveloping the whole country, the Committee has
come to note that the literature prepared and the programmes initiated are neither related to the local needs of the people nor the
local dialects.  Half of India’s population is illiterate.  One aspect on which one can feel happy is that the AIDS syndrome has
not yet touched, in a bigger way, the horizons of the rural areas.  This is, therefore the area which is to be protected with very
well chalked out programmes.  The programmes to be launched should take into view the local people’s conditions, their
cultural behaviour and the language.  Unless the message transmitted is not properly received the whole effort will go waste. 
The Committee strongly recommends the Department to give a serious consideration on this.  The Committee is of the view that
in the awareness programme, participation of NGOs, students, local bodies etc. should be given preference to the maximum
extent because these are the groups which can effectively transmit the message through the language understandable to the local
community.
Reply of Government
3.5        During the last five years, the National AIDS Control Programme has successfully created awareness among the public
about HIV/AIDS through mass media campaigns, community mobilization and HIV/AIDS education in schools and colleges. 
All media of communication, including interpersonal communication are being used to disseminate AIDS prevention messages
in rural and urban areas.  The State Governments conduct awareness programmes through mass media campaigns as well as
traditional art forms in order to ensure that awareness programmes are in the local medium and bear the regional sensitivities in
mind.
The National AIDS Control Organisation also provides budgetary support to the media units under the aegis of Ministry of
Information and Broadcasting, viz. Doordarshan, All India Radio.  Song and Drama Division, Directorate of Field Publicity,
Press Information Bureau and Films Division.
-
                      The Directorate of Field Publicity has a network of 260 Field Units spread over all States and Union Territories.  All
these units are involved in organising AIDS awareness activities including film shows and programmes of seminars, elocution
contests, question-answer sessions, and debates, quiz compositions, rallies and workshops.
-                      The Song and Drama Division organizes dance-drama shows and folk media performances in rural areas through its
regional centres.
-                      The Directorate of Advertising and Visual Publicity (DAVP) produced more than a dozen video spots and jingles. 
These along with the spots produced through a professional agency are being telecast on a regular basis on Doordarshan.
-
                      Generic material such as posters, pamphlets, booklets, films has been designed at the central level and disseminated to
the States, UTs, NGOs and the media thus ensuring broad coverage and  quality and the correctness of the messages.  This
material has been brought out in eleven regional languages in order to relate to the local needs of the people or the local dialects.
 
-                      NACO is collaborating with the Department of Women and Child Development to integrate HIV/AIDS awareness with
the ICDS programme in order to generate awareness at the grassroots level.  To overcome the barriers of illiteracy, the
awareness material will have a high visual content.
Recommendation
5.5        The Committee expresses its concern over the fact that a large number of blood banks are existing in this country
without basic facilities for testing.  The Committee while appreciating the recent steps taken for issuing licenses to the blood
banks has been informed that they also use unstandardised kits and there is no uniform kit available for testing.  The Committee,
therefore, feels that the screening method for Hepatitis B must be properly standardised.  The Committee is aware that law
already exists where under-screening is mandatory for blood banks.  What is sadly lacking is non-implementation of this
mandatory requirement.  The Committee feels that it is the duty of the Government to find ways and means for getting this
provision implemented effectively all over the country.
Reply of Government
5.5  It is mandatory for all blood banks in the country to screen each and every unit of blood for HIV, Hepatitis 'B', Malaria and
Syphllis.  It is being monitored regularly through States and Union Territories.

5.6        The Committee also notes that the medical and paramedical staff, who are working in rural areas are not trained to
perform the test.  The Department should focus its attention in giving specialised training to the medical and para medical

Reply of Government
5.6 The ability to perform the test in the rural areas will depend on availability of trained manpower, physical infrastructure such
as suitably equipped laboratory and funds for procurement of diagnostic kits.  National Institute of Communicable Diseases
(NICD), as a part of the National Surveillance Programme for Communicable Diseases, is training Lab. Technicians at district

National AIDS Control Organisation has developed a comprehensive training programme for all health care workers from

Recommendation
3.2              The Committee is pained to note that a number of States have not filled in the sanctioned posts.   The reason given that
this has been done in view of the fact that the National AIDS Control Programme is a time bound project, is not convincing to
the Committee.   The Committee feels that this aspect could have been tackled by the Centre in a better manner by convincing
the states about the importance of the programme and the necessity of creation of the posts and a via-media for the continuance
of the posts created could have been found out.   It is surprising for the Committee that the Department has not done anything in
this regard till now.   This aspect needs to be considered immediately and all the States should be asked to create the number of
posts as are required.
Reply of Government
3.2        In the first phase of the National AIDS Control Programme, 17 posts were sanctioned in large states and 11 posts in
small states/UTs for programme management at state level but due to various reasons, these posts could not be filled by the
State Governments.   Government of India had reminded states/UTs in this regard from time to time.
For the effective implementation of second phase of National AIDS Control Programme, Government of India has
sanctioned 47 posts for major States, 39 for medium States and 27 for small States/UTs which also includes posts to be filled on
contractual basis.  The States are in the process of filling up these posts.   All the States/UTs have given an undertaking to fill up
the sanctioned posts.
Comments of the Committee
The Committee was informed that out of 1143 posts sanctioned under NACP Phase II, which started in
November, 1999, 542 posts have already been filled up till June, 2000.  The Committee is, however, disturbed to note that
information with regard to vacancy position in respect of States/UTs like Madhya Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Tripura and D
& N Haveli is not available with the Central Government.  What is more alarming is that in the case of many major and
medium states, number of posts filled up so far is very less.  The Committee has been given to understand that the main
reasons for vacant posts are non-availability of suitable candidates in some states as well as the time taken in filling up
the posts either through deputation or on contract.  There has also been some reluctance on the part of the States to fill
up these posts on the ground that the employees would become the permanent liability of the State Govt.  after the
closure of the project.
            The Committee feels that given the menace of AIDS, which will only increase in future, the approach of Central
Govt. would not do any good to the morale of the persons who are instrumental in the implementation of the programme
at grass root level.  The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier observation that this aspect could have been tackled
by the Govt. in a better manner by convincing the States about the importance of the Programme and the urgent

necessity of creation of posts.  The Committee once again emphasises that keeping in view the financial  status of State
Govts. a via-media for continuance of the posts beyond the Project Period has to be found out by the Govt. without any
further delay. 
 
 
Recommendation
3.3               The Committee was given to understand that IMA and NACO are making a combined effort to train general medical
practitioners for clinical management of AIDS  and HIV infected persons.   The training given is too less to cover a chunk of
general physicians in the country, particularly in the states where AIDS and HIV are rampant.   A large-scale training to the
physicians and nurses is required so that they may be able to effectively tackle the patients.   The Committee is also given to
understand that many physicians and nurses do not turn up or attend to the HIV and AIDS patients mainly because of the lack of
general awareness and the skills to treat and tackle them.   Therefore, the Department should chalk out a massive scheme to
cover, at least once, for some period for training most of the general physicians in the major cities of the country.   Nurse
training is also not very satisfactory.   They need to be given specialized skill training.
Reply of Government
3.3        Government of India has chalked out a comprehensive training programme to cover medical and para-medical workers
including nurses to train them in prevention and control of HIV and AIDS.   A programme for training of General Medical
Practitioners was also developed for which a sum of Rs. 37 lakhs was sanctioned  to central office of Indian Medical
Association.  So  far, they have trained 7500 physicians in different parts of the country.   The association is being requested to
take up more training programmes.   Besides  Indian Medical Association, Christian Medical Association of India (CMAI) and
Voluntary Health Association of India (VHAI) had also taken up training programmes for general medical practitioners on HIV
and AIDS prevention and control.   The curriculum of training courses includes the management of HIV infected people and
AIDS cases and their counselling.   In order to update the knowledge of Medical Practitioners on management of Sexually
Transmitted Diseases, 1.5 lakh booklets on Syndromic Management on Sexually Transmitted Diseases have been mailed to all
the members of Indian Medical Association.
            During second phase of National AIDS Control Programme, three tier saturation Training Programme has been
initiated.  At tertiary health care line, which includes medical colleges/regional institutions, persons have been trained.  To each
institution a team of 10 faculty members from deptt. of medicine, surgery, Obstertic & Gynecology, Pediatric, microbiology,
public health, blood banking, social science/Psychiatry and Sexually transmitted diseases have been trained.  This team will
train the other medical and paramedical functionaries at institutional level, as well as training of district level core team of
trainers which in turn train medical, paramedical and other auxiliary staff functioning at district & Primary Health Centre level.
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee has been informed that during the IInd Phse of NACP, 4412 doctors(specialists/medical officers),
5874 nurses and 5948 para-medicals have been trained at various levels by States/UTs and other organisations like Steel
Authority of India Limited (SAIL), Railways, ESI Corporation etc.  The Committee also finds that in majority of the
States, medical personnel have been trained as `Core Trainers’.  However, as per the figures furnished to the Committee,
States/UTs like Andhra Pradesh, Lakshadeep, Maharashtra, Pondicherry, Tripura and West Bengal have not taken any
initiative in this regard.  What is more disturbing is that in States/UTs like Goa, Gujarat, Haryana, J & K, Karnataka,
Kerala, M.P., Meghalaya, Nagaland, Orissa, U.P., D & N Haveli, Damman and Diu, work of training of Medical
Peronnel seems to have ended with the grooming of Core Trainers.  Not only this, a very negligible number of
medical/paramedical personnel have been trained in HIV/AIDS so far and that too is concentrated in very few states of
the Country.  The Committee is constrined to observe that training which is the most vital component of AIDS Control
Programme seems to be still in the initial stages.  It is all the more essential and urgent in view of inherent reservations
in the minds of a large number of doctors and nurses to handle HIV/AIDS patients.  While appreciating the role of
Indian Medical Association (IMA), Christian Medical Association of India (CMAI) and Voluntary Health Association of
India (VHAI), the Committee strongly feels that private organisations alone cannot handle this massive programme. 
Co-ordinated effort with an active role to be played by both Central and State Govts. would be the ideal position. 
Monitoring of the training programme at regular intervals is bound to achieve the desired results.
Recommendation
3.4               The Committee understands that blood banks are the area which needs to be strengthened and modernized for securing
safe blood supply.  Blood banks are the place from where infected blood is donated and transfused.   The Committee is,

however, constrained to note that many blood banks in the public sector are yet to be taken up for modernisation to achieve the
goal of securing safe blood supply.   All the blood banks, at least in the public sector, should be immediately covered to ensure
supply of safe blood.   The Committee also feels the necessity of a regular monitoring of the public sector blood banks on any
possible violation of norms.  Similarly, the Committee is equally concerned about the blood banks in the private sector.   There
is hardly any monitoring over the activities of the private blood banks.   Efforts are also required to modernize Government
blood banks and provide necessary facilities for testing  AIDS/HIV etc.   Similarly, Government should also see to it that the
recently amended Drugs and Cosmetics Rule which provides that no blood bank shall collect blood from professional donors, is
strictly adhered to by al the blood banks.
Reply OF Government
3.4        Government of India has provided for modernization of 727 blood banks in public sector and 88 blood banks in
voluntary sector.   It is mandatory for all the blood banks to obtain license from Drug Controller General of India before making
it operational.  Currently there are 1352 licensed blood banks in the country.   There is complete ban on professional blood
donation since 1.1.98.   It is mandatory for each licensed blood bank to test blood units for HIV, Hepatitis B, Syphilis and
Malaria.   For the monitoring of the proper functioning of blood banks in States there is the Department of Food and Drugs,
which conducts regular inspections of these blood banks, and the renewal of annual license is recommended by them on the
basis of their inspection reports.   State AIDS Control Societies are also conducting regular visits of the blood banks in their
respective states to maintain the quality of these blood banks.
Further Comments
On a specific query about the number of blood banks, whose licenses have not been renewed during the last five years
and the nature of irregularities found during the inspection, the Committee was informed that in the last five years, 176 license
applications for blood banks were rejected and five renewal applications were not approved.  The main
deficiencies/irregularities were : I) inadequate storage facility ii) deficiency in testing procedure and facility iii) suspected
dependence on professional paid blood donors iv) lack of qualified technical personnel, etc.
Comments of the Committee
While noting that blood-related infection has come down from 8 percent to 4 percent, the Committee is of the
view that the role played by blood banks both in public and private sector is very vital in the containment of HIV/AIDS. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that expeditious steps should be taken by the Department to modernize all the
licensed blood banks both in public and private sector.  The Committee, while appreciating the appointment of a Joint
Controller of Blood Safety on a full time basis in every AIDS Control Society in the Country, is of the view that an
effective monitoring mechanism needs to be built up without any delay.  This is all the more essential in the case of
private blood banks which are alleged to be entertaining professional donors in large numbers.  Both regular and
random checks should be carried out to be followed by remedial measures.  The Committee notes that voluntary blood
donation is increasing  gradually.  The Committee, however, feels that with the active involvement of voluntary agencies,
public awareness can be increased in this regard.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should
take effective steps in this matter.
Recommendation
3.9        NGOs have to very vital role in AIDS Control Program.  They are the groups which can work in close proximity to the
people particularly the high risk behavioural groups.  The  Committee, however, is constrained to notethat the Central
Government which sanctions funds to the NGOs does not have even the list of NGOs working under the programme in various
states.  The Committee feels that Centre should take initiative in bringing the NGOs forward under the implementation of the
programme.
Reply of Government
3.9        NACO has developed a directory of NGOs working on HIV/AIDS prevention and control, which is continuously being
updated.  Information is being collected through the State AIDS Programme Officers, bilateral andUN agencies for this purpose.
NACO is adopting various measures to include the participation of NGOs, in designing and implementing HIV/AIDS related
programmes and policies and programmes.  Under the NACO programme, guidelines have been formulated for NGO funding
and to encourage partnerships between the State AIDS Cell and NGOs.  Separate guidelines have been formulated to help the
NGOs intervene at the community level.
NACO also organized a National Workshop with NGOs on HIV/AIDS.  The workshop which was held on 15-16
th
January, 98 was attended by representatives of 150 NGOs, bilateral and UN agencies.  The main objective of this National level
workshop was to involve the NGOs inthe policy framework of the second phase of the programme by re-examining the

procedures, policies and roles for collaboration between NGOs, the bilateral agencies and the Government.
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee notes that a directory of NGOs working on HIV/AIDS Prevention and Control has been
developed by NACO which is being continuously updated.  While appreciating the various measures taken by NACO for
participation of NGOs, the Committee has a word of caution.  It has been observed that NGOs are by and large
concentrated in Metropolitan cities so as to get wider publicity for their activities.  The Committee feels that NGOs
should also come forward to work in rural areas as the menace of AIDS has started affecting rural masses also.  The
Committee, therefore, recommends that efforts should be made by the Govt. so as to encourage NGOs to work both in
urban and rural areas.  While encouraging the participation of NGOs in AIDS Prevention and Control Programme, an
effective monitoring mechanism for supervising their activities also needs to be evolved so that only those NGOs
performing well remain in the field.
Recommendation
3.13      The fact that there being no cure for AIDS is agitating the mind of scientific community the world over.   Whatever
medicines that are available are only to give temporary relief.  Even those medicines are not available to a large number of
infected population because of the high cost.  The Committee is pained to learn from the representative of the Ministry of Health
and Family Welfare that there is no company which is importing the drugs.  Even if the Government does not want to introduce
the drugs for treatment, efforts should at least be made to ensure the availability of the drugs in the market.   The Committee
recommends that the Government should consider this and see that medicines which are available in other parts of the world are
brought/made available in India at a cheaper cost.   The Committee was also given to understand  that the Indian systems of
medicines such as Ayurveda and Homoeopathy claim to have got medicines for curing AIDS.  Government should seriously
examine and have research done on the efficacy of all those medicines as early as possible.   This is all the more necessary
because if indigenous medicines are found to be efficacious these could be made available at a cheaper cost.
Reply of Government
3.13            Under the National AIDS Control programme, funds are provided to states and UTs for the management of
opportunistic infections in HIV/AIDS patients.   As far as the Anti-Retro-viral drugs are concerned,  they are not provided under
the programme.   However, drugs like Azidothymidine, Lamivudine, Indinavir, Saquinavir and Ritonavir etc. are available in the
market.
Government of India has provided funds to Central Council of Research on Homeopathy for conducting trials of homeopathy
drugs in HIV/AIDS patients to assess their efficacy.   The research is in progress and the final report is still awaited.  Funds have
also been provided by the Tamil Nadu State AIDS Control Society to Institute of Thoracic Medicine,  Tambram to study the
efficacy of Sidha drugs in management of HIV/AIDS cases.  The Final report is still awaited.
Comments of the Committee
The Committee notes that drugs like Azidothymidine, Lamivudine, Indinavir, Saquinavir and Ritonaviv etc. for
treatment of AIDS/HIV are available in the market. However, the Committee apprehends that these drugs due to their
prohibitive cost must be out of the reach of majority of patients.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that serious
efforts need to be made by the Govt. so as to ensure the availability of these drugs in India at a cheaper cost.  If need be,
Patent Laws should be looked into for finding a solution to this problem.
 The Committee notes that funds have been provided for conducting research to study the efficacy of
homoeopathy and Sidha drugs in management of HIV/AIDS cases.  The Committee hopes that this research work would
lead to some positive results for HIV/AIDS Patients.
Recommendation
5.1        The Committee is constrained to note that the country has 40 million carriers of HBV and the Government has not
woken up yet to meet the challenge.  Even though some steps have been taken by the Department, they are far from adequate. 
The Committee is of the view that prevention is better than cure.  During the course of its interaction with experts, it was
emphasised again and again that mass vaccination was the only foolproof method for eradication of this ever spreading disease. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that it should be taken up by the Government, on a large scale and steps should be taken
by the Government to include it in the universal immunisation programme.  Taking into account the fact that WHO has
recommended that countries with a carrier prevalence of 2 percent and above should consider inclusion of HBV in routine
immunisation programme for infants and as India has a prevalence of 4 percent, the Committee feels that vaccination
programme should be started without further delay.

NINETY-NINTH REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/99threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:13:15]
Recommendation
5.2 This measure becomes all the more necessary keeping in view the fact that infants and young children who generally have
mild infection, can become life-long carriers without showing any symptoms all along.  And after 20-25 years about 25 percent
of chronic carriers can develop hepatitis cirrhosis (liver failure) and liver cancer.  The Committee feels that successful
implementation of pulse polio programme can be taken up as a role model for starting vaccination programme for Hepatitis B. 
The Committee is constrained to note that the proposal to include vaccination against Hepatitis B can only be implemented if
adequate resources become available during the 9 th plan.  The Committee feels that this is a sorry state of affairs.  Government
has to provide sufficient funds during 9th plan period, if future generations are to be saved. 
Reply of Government
5.1. Since health is a State subject, it is the responsibility of the State Government to take measures for the prevention of all
diseases.  However,  Hepatitis B was considered in the Department of Family Welfare for inclusion in the Immunization
Programme while formulating Plan of Action for the 9th Plan.  The initial estimate which was worked out is as follows:-
a.             Estimated no. of newborn - 2.5 crore
b.             No. of doses to be administered - 3 doses.
c.             No. of doses required including wastage - 10.00 crore
d.             Approx. cost per dose at international rate - Rs.50/-
e.             Total fund requirement - Rs. 500 crores/year.
 
However, the Planning Commission had indicated that additional allocation of funds will not be possible.  Therefore, the same
could not be included in the final plan of action of the 9
th Plan.
The Department of Family Welfare is still actively involved in the consultation process with experts, Indian Council of
Medical Research, International Organizations for modalities of introduction of the vaccine, and also looking for the funding
sources from World Bank etc.
Further Comments
            In reply to a question as to what efforts have so far been made by the Department to generate additional funds,   the
Department replied that introduction of Hepatitis B in the Universal Immunization Programme  (UIP) has not been possible due
to the enormous financial implication of such a step.   The Planning Commission has stated that funds will have to be found
within the existing plan resources of the Department of Health for the 9 th Plan.   While steps are being explored for formulating
a pilot project, including Hepatitis B under the Universal Immunization Programme (UIP) is a step which will require large
scale resource mobilization.   This does not appear to be feasible during the 9th plan period.
Comments of the Committee
 The Committee is of the view that Hepatitis B is even more dangerous that AIDS in terms of its             infectious
nature and spread amongst 40 million people.   Mass vaccination is the only fool proof method for preventing this ever
spreading disease.   The Committee, therefore,  reiterates its recommendation that the Department should not only
pursue this matter with the Planning Commission but it should also look for funds from other sources.
Recommendation
5.3        The Committee feels that apart from vaccination there are some other areas where there is a chance of spreading HBV
which cannot be ignored like rampant use of unsterilised syringes in hospitals.   This unethical practice was more rampant in
rural areas.   Mere issuing guidelines to state authorities for the use of a separate sterile syringe and needle for each injection
would not suffice.   The Committee feels that stringent measures are required to check this dangerous practice.   Steps should
also be taken to educate the general masses about fatal consequences of such use of unsterlised syringes.
Reply of Government
5.3        National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) has initiated a comprehensive training programme for all categories of
the Health Care Workers on universal precautions to prevent the spread of HIV, Hepatitis 'B' and other blood borne infections in
all Government hospitals/Health Centers.  Besides, the information on this aspect is also being disseminated to the community
through media.

NINETY-NINTH REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/99threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:13:15]
Further Comments
TheCommittee specifically wanted to knowthe measures taken by the Govt. to ensure the use of separate sterile syringe
and needle for each injection.  The Department replied that the following two measures have been takenso far:-
-                      instructions issued  by DGHS toall Central Govt. hospitals as well as State Govts. for use of separate sterile
syringe and needle for each injection .
-                      Training of doctors , nurses and para-medical personnel of hospitals etc regarding the use of separate syringes
and needles for each injection under the AIDS programme.
Comments of the Committee
The Committee is of the view that these instructions lack the necessary  teeth to stop the unethical practice of use of 
unsterilised syringes in hospitals. Moreover, the Committee also feels that merely by issuing instructions to the hospitals
or by training doctors and para-medicals, this unethical practice perhaps would not be contained.  Hence, it reiterates its
earlier observation that stringent measures are required to check this dangerous practice.    The Committee feels that
exemplary punishment to defaulters would set an example for others.  Steps should also be taken to educate the general
masses about fatal consequences of use of unsterlised syringes and needles.  The Committee is also of the view that an
effective monitoring mechanism of random checks to be carried out right from PHCs to big hospitals in the cities can
yield the desired results.

Indian Medical Association (IMA), Christian Medical Association of India (CMAI) and Voluntary Health Association of
India (VHAI), the Committee strongly feels that private organisations alone cannot handle this massive programme. 
Co-ordinated effort with an active role to be played by both Central and State Govts. would be the ideal position. 
Monitoring of the training programme at regular intervals is bound to achieve the desired results. (Para 3.3)
Comments of the Committee
While noting that blood-related infection has come down from 8 percent to 4 percent, the Committee is of the
view that the role played by blood banks both in public and private sector is very vital in the containment of HIV/AIDS. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that expeditious steps should be taken by the Department to modernize all the
licensed blood banks both in public and private sector.  The Committee, while appreciating the appointment of a Joint
Controller of Blood Safety on a full time basis in every AIDS Control Society in the Country, is of the view that an
effective monitoring mechanism needs to be built up without any delay.  This is all the more essential in the case of
private blood banks which are alleged to be entertaining professional donors in large numbers.  Both regular and
random checks should be carried out to be followed by remedial measures.  The Committee notes that voluntary blood
donation is increasing  gradually.  The Committee, however, feels that with the active involvement of voluntary agencies,
public awareness can be increased in this regard.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should
take effective steps in this matter.       (Para 3.4)
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee notes that a directory of NGOs working on HIV/AIDS Prevention and Control has been
developed by NACO which is being continuously updated.  While appreciating the various measures taken by NACO for
participation of NGOs, the Committee has a word of caution.  It has been observed that NGOs are by and large
concentrated in Metropolitan cities so as to get wider publicity for their activities.  The Committee feels that NGOs
should also come forward to work in rural areas as the menace of AIDS has started affecting rural masses also.  The
Committee, therefore, recommends that efforts should be made by the Govt. so as to encourage NGOs to work both in
urban and rural areas.  While encouraging the participation of NGOs in AIDS Prevention and Control Programme, an
effective monitoring mechanism for supervising their activities also needs to be evolved so that only those NGOs
performing well remain in the field.    (Para 3.9)
Comments of the Committee
The Committee notes that drugs like Azidothymidine, Lamivudine, Indinavir, Saquinavir and Ritonaviv etc. for
treatment of AIDS/HIV are available in the market. However, the Committee apprehends that these drugs due to their
prohibitive cost must be out of the reach of majority of patients.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that serious
efforts need to be made by the Govt. so as to ensure the availability of these drugs in India at a cheaper cost.  If need be,
Patent Laws should be looked into for finding a solution to this problem.
 The Committee notes that funds have been provided for conducting research to study the efficacy of
homoeopathy and Sidha drugs in management of HIV/AIDS cases.  The Committee hopes that this research work would
lead to some positive results for HIV/AIDS Patients. (Para 3.13)
Comments of the Committee
 The Committee is of the view that Hepatitis B is even more dangerous that AIDS in terms of its            
infectious nature and spread amongst 40 million people.   Mass vaccination is the only fool proof method for preventing
this ever spreading disease.   The Committee, therefore,  reiterates its recommendation that the Department should not
only pursue this matter with the Planning Commission but it should also look for funds from other sources.  (Para 5.1)
 
Comments of the Committee
The Committee is of the view that these instructions lack the necessary  teeth to stop the unethical practice of use
of  unsterilised syringes in hospitals. Moreover, the Committee also feels that merely by issuing instructions to the
hospitals or by training doctors and para-medicals, this unethical practice perhaps would not be contained.  Hence, it
reiterates its earlier observation that stringent measures are required to check this dangerous practice.    The Committee
feels that exemplary punishment to defaulters would set an example for others.  Steps should also be taken to educate the
general masses about fatal consequences of use of unsterlised syringes and needles.  The Committee is also of the view
that an effective monitoring mechanism of random checks to be carried out right from PHCs to big hospitals in the cities
can yield the desired results. (Para 5.3)

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Standing Committee on Energy having been
authorised by the Committee to present the Report on their behalf,
present this First Report (Fourteenth Lok Sabha) on Demands for Grants
(2004-05) relating to the Ministry of Power.
2. The Committee took evidence of the representatives of the
Ministry of Power on 12th August, 2004.
3. The Committee wish to thank the representatives of the Ministry
of Power who appeared before the Committee and placed their
considered views. They also wish to thank the Ministry of Power for
furnishing the replies on the points raised by the Committee.
4. The Report was considered and adopted by the Committee at
their sitting held on 18th August, 2004.
5. For facility of reference and convenience, the observations and
recommendations of the Committee have been printed in bold letters
in the body of the Report.
   N
EW D ELHI; GURUDAS KAMAT,
18 August, 2004 Chairman,
27 Sravana, 1926 (Saka) Standing Committee on Energy.

REPORT
PART I
CHAPTER I
INTRODUCTORY
The Ministry of Power started functioning independently with effect
from 2nd July, 1992. Earlier it was known as the Ministry of Energy
comprising the Departments of Power, Coal and Non-Conventional
Energy Sources.
1.2 Electricity is a concurrent subject at Entry 38 in List III of the
Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India. The Ministry of Power
is primarily responsible for the development of electrical energy in the
country. The Ministry is concerned with perspective planning, policy
formulation, processing of projects for investment decision, monitoring
of the implementation of power projects, training and manpower
development and the administration and enactment of legislation in
regard to thermal, hydro power generation, transmission and
distribution.
1.3 The Ministry of Power is entrusted with the evolution of the
general policy in the field of Energy. Under the Allocation of Business
Rules, the Ministry is responsible for the following :
(i) General policy in the electric power sector and issues relating
to energy policy. (details of short, medium and long-term
policies in terms of formulation, acceptance, implementation
and review of such policies, cutting across sectors, fuels
regions and cross-country flows).
(ii) All matters relating to hydro-electric power (except small/
mini/micro hydel projects of and below 25 MW capacity)
and thermal power and transmission system network.
(iii) Research, development and technical assistance relating to
hydro-electric and thermal power and transmission system
network.

2
(iv) Administration of the Electricity Act, 2003 (34 of 2003) and
Energy Conservation Act, 2001, the Damodar Valley
Corporation Act, 1948 (14 of 1948) and Bhakra Beas
Management Board as provided in Punjab Reorganization
Act, 1966 (31 of 1966)
(v) All matters relating to Central Electricity Authority and
Central Electricity Regulatory Commission.
(vi) Rural Electrification Power Schemes in Union Territories and
issues relating to power supply in the States and Union
Territories.
(vii) Administrative control of Public Sector Undertakings,
Statutory and Autonomous Bodies functioning under the
Ministry.
(viii) Other Public Sector Enterprises concerned with the subject
included under this Ministry except such projects as are
specifically allotted to anyother Ministry or Department.
(ix) All matters concerning energy conservation and energy
efficiency pertaining to Power Sector.
1.4 In all technical and economic matters, Ministry of Power is
assisted by the central Electricity Authority (CEA). While the Authority
(CEA)is a Statutory Body constituted under the erstwhile Electricity
(Supply) Act, 1948, hereinafter replaced by the Electricity Act, 2003,
where similar provisions exists, the office of the CEA is an “Attached
Office” of the Ministry of Power. The CEA is responsible for technical
coordination and supervision of programmes and is also entrusted
with a number of statutory functions. It is headed by a Chairman,
who is also ex-officio Secretary to the Government of India and
comprises six full time Members of the CEA of the rank of ex-officio
Additional Secretaries to the Government of India. They are designated
as Member (Thermal), Member (Hydro), Member (Economic &
Commercial), Member (Power Systems), Member (Planning) and
Member (Grid Operation and Distribution).
1.5 Following the enactment of the Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission’s Act (1998) since submerged in Electricity Act, 2003 the
Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) was constituted in
July, 1998 with a Chairman & three full time members. The main
functions of the CERC are to regulate tariff of Centrally owned or
controlled generating companies, regulate inter-state transmission

3
including tariff of transmission entities, to regulate inter-state Bulk Sale
of Power, to advise the Central government in matters of tariff
formulation policy etc.
1.6 Badarpur Management Contract Cell (BMCC) is a subordinate
office directly under the control of Ministry of Power and 13
subordinate offices under the control of Central Electricity Authority.
1.7 There are four Statutory Bodies, six Public Sector Undertakings,
two Joint Venture Corporations, two Autonomous Bodies (Societies)
and two other Organizations under the administrative control of the
Ministry. These are :
I. Statutory Bodies
(i) Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC),
New Delhi.
(ii) Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC), Calcutta;
(iii) Bhakra Beas Management Board (BBMB), Chandigarh;
(iv) Bureau of Energy Efficiency, (BEE), New Delhi.
II. Public Sector Undertakings
(i) Rural Electrification Corporation (REC), New Delhi;
(ii) National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC), New Delhi;
(iii) National Hydro-electric Power Corporation (NHPC),
Faridabad;
(iv) North-Eastern Electric Power Corporation (NEEPCO),
Shillong;
(v) Power Finance Corporation (PFC), New Delhi;
(vi) Power Grid Corporation of India Ltd. (PGCIL), New Delhi.
III. Joint Venture Corporations
(i) Satluj Jal Vidyut Nigam Limited (SJVN), Shimla;
(ii) Tehri Hydro Development Corporation (THDC), Noida (UP);
IV . Autonomous Bodies
(i) Central Power Research Institute (CPRI), Bangalore;
(ii) National Power Training Institute (NPTI), Faridabad.

4
V . Other Organisations
(i) Narmada Hydro Development Corporation (NHDC), Bhopal
(MP) A joint venture of NHPC & Government of Madhya
Pradesh.
(ii) Power Trading Corporation (PTC), New Delhi.
1.8 The Committee observe that from 1712 MW of power generation
during 1950, 11,2508 MW of power is being generated sine March,
2004 in the country. The per capita consumption of electricity in India
is less than 1000 KWh/year as compared to 8000 to 13000 KWh/year
in the developed countries like Japan, France, Australia and USA.
Further, against the all India average of 43.52% household electrification,
the Committee note that States like Bihar and Jharkhand have below
10% of the household electrified so far.
1.9 Against the total installed power generation capacity of 112706
MW in India, 29625 MW is hydro power, 78492 MW is thermal, 2720
MW is nuclear and 1869 MW is wind power. Further, against the 8th
Plan target of 30538 MW the actual achievements were 16422 MW.
During 9th Plan 19015 MW of additional capacity of power generation
was created against the target of 40245 MW. The Committee observe
that 41110 MW power capacity targets have been fixed. For 10th Plan
7458 MW of the targeted capacity addition has already been achieved
and projects with capacity of 27891 MW are reported under execution/
implementation. The Government have initiated 50000 MW hydro-
electric initiatives to cover pre-feasibility reports for 162 hydro-electric
projects.
1.10 The Committee observe that the total Plan outlay for power
sector (Ministry of Power) during 9th Plan were drastically reduced
from an allocation of Rs. 45591.05 crore to Rs. 39454.31 crore. The total
10th Plan outlay for power sector are Rs. 1,43399.00 crore. The
Committee further note that downsizing of the Plan outlays has not
stopped yet. The Plan outlays for 2002-03 were reduced to Rs. 11268.26
crore at the RE stage from Rs. 13483.00 crore originally allocated. The
actuals during 2002-03 were Rs. 8649.00 crore. The Committee find
that the Central Plan outlays for the year 2003-04 had undergone
revision from Rs. 14668.00 crore to Rs. 12038.00 crore due to reasons
such as delay in sanction of projects of NHPC, non-approval of new
schemes of DVC/NEEPCO/Ministry of Power, etc. The Plan outlays
for the year 2004-05 are Rs. 15630.00 crore including Rs. 12030.00 as
IEBR and Rs. 3600.00 crore as gross budgetary support.

5
1.11 The Committee also observe that there are huge T&D losses
largely due to theft and un-metered supply and account for Rs. 20,000
crore annually. In this connection, the Committee note that the
Government is implementing APDRP Scheme to improve sub-
transmission and distribution system. Further, for accelerated
electrification of all the villages and all the households the definition
of ‘village electrification’ has been suitably modified. The funds
requirement to provide electricity to all the villages and access to
households is estimated at around Rs. 16,000 crore.
1.12 As of now there is huge gap between demand and supply of
the electricity in the country which varies from State to State. To reduce
this gap, the Ministry have taken a number of States. Apart from
adding new generation capacity, it has undertaken R&M and RLA
works as well as taken steps for demand side management through
energy conservation measures.
1.13 The Committee have scrutinized the detailed Demands for
Grants of the Ministry for the year 2004-05 vis-a-vis performance of
various programmes during 2003-04. The Committee place on record
their appreciation where the Ministry have been able to utilise its
Grants to a large extent. The Committee approve the Demands for
Grants of the Ministry of Power 2004-05 subject to their observations
and recommendations which are contained in the succeeding Chapter.

2.10 The Committee are perturbed to note that the Ministry of
Power projected higher Plan outlays during the years 2002-03 and

12
2003-04 which were drastically reduced at RE stage. From the plan
outlays of the Ministry of Power, the Committee observe that for
the year 2002-03, these were reduced from Rs. 13483.00 crore at
B.E. stage to Rs. 11268.36 crore at RE stage. The Ministry could not
utilize this reduced amount and the actuals were Rs. 8649.22 crore
only. Thus, the Ministry of Power surrendered an amount of
Rs. 4833.78 crore during 2002-03 against the budgeted outlays. Further,
the Plan Outlays of the Ministry for 2003-04 were Rs. 14667.61 crore
comprising of Rs. 3500.00 crore as GBS and Rs. 11167.61 crore as
IEBR. This was reduced to Rs. 12037.77 crore at RE stage comprising
of Rs. 1850 crore as GBS and Rs. 10187.77 crore as IEBR. The actual
utilization of funds during 2003-04 was Rs. 10741.00 and the Ministry
of Power surrendered an amount of Rs. 3927.00 crore as compared to
BE for the year. Thus, in both the last two financial years, the
Ministry failed to utilise the budgeted amount. The Committee are
not satisfied with the reasons furnished by the Government for non-
utilisation of the amount. The scheme of NERLDC by Power Grid
is said to have been completed at lesser cost and resulted in saving
of Rs. 29.87 crore. Better and advance budgeting would have ensured
that the surrendered amount could have been utilised for other
schemes. Similarly, the Committee are dismayed to note that in case
of NHPC (2002-03) an amount of Rs. 742.72 crore was surrendered
due to non-approval of Purulia Pump Storage, Kirshanganga, Parbati-
III, Chamera III, capitalization of IDC, etc. The National Power
Training Institute (NPTI) and Central Power Research Institute (CPRI)
surrendered an amount of Rs. 19.5 crore and 23.52 crore respectively
out of a total outlays of Rs. 24.60 crore and Rs. 25.00 crore due to
non-approval of new schemes and slow progress of ongoing schemes
during 2002-03. The Committee find that new schemes of the Ministry
of Power for which funds to the tune of Rs. 20.00 crore were
provided, could not get approved and the full amount for the purpose
was surrendered during 2002-03. Further, due to non-approval of the
revised cost estimates of the Tehri Stage-I by the competent authority
and reluctance of the Northern Region constituents to source Power
from Tehri Project, an amount of Rs. 391.56 crore was surrendered
against the total outlays of Rs. 467.31 crore. Thus, it would be seen
that a large number of schemes planned by the Ministry could not
get even initial approval to start. This shows that those schemes
were not planned by the Ministry perfectly and for which the scarce
resources of the Government were blocked. The Committee do not
approve the present practice being followed by the Ministry of Power
which have been asking for higher allocations year after year, but
the implementation of plans and policies are poor as ground realities

13
are not taken into account while formulating and implementing the
plans. The Committee feel that with such a state of affairs the scarce
resources remain locked in unproductive returns at the cost of other
needy sectors of the economy. The Committee are pained to note
that although they have repeatedly recommended for formulation of
realistic plans but no action seems to has been taken by the
Government on these recommendations. The Committee, however,
expect that intensified monitoring mechanism which is being put in
place by the Ministry of Power will ensure that budgeted amounts
earmarked at the BE stage is fully utilised during 2004-05. At the
same time, the Committee desire that the Government should review
all the on-going schemes in the month of July-August and if required,
re-allocate the funds so that the budgeted amount is utilised fully
during the financial year.
2.11 The Committee further observe the quarterly utilization of
funds by the Ministry of Power against the GBS of Rs. 3500 crore
and IEBR of Rs. 11167.61 crore during 2003-04. The quarterly
comparison with preceding year indicate that expenditure during first
3 quarters of the financial year are very low and it is only in the
last quarter, the percentage utilization of funds is above the normal.
Taking note of various ongoing projects/schemes of the Ministry of
Power which are completed in a time span of three to ten years, the
Committee fail to understand as to why there is rush for utilization
of funds in the last quarter of the financial year. The Committee are
of the view that this unhealthy trend of not spending any amount
during first quarter of the financial year and rushing to major
expenditure in the last quarter, especially in the month of February
and March is against the financial norms. The Committee are of the
concerned opinion that there has been system failure on large-scale
in such cases. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommend the
Government that a meaningful and relevant programmes and policies
be formulated so that there should be regular infusion of funds in
various projects/schemes in all quarters of the financial year and the
total plan outlays are fully utilized. The Committee would like to
be apprised of the action taken by the Government in this regard.

investment approval by the competent authority for each new project.
The Committee in their 40th Report [Para No. 2.11 (13th Lok Sabha)]

had observed that as per the existing procedure in vogue, each
thermal power project costing more than Rs. 2500.00 crore is appraised
by the Central Electricity Authority. Similarly, the limit for hydro
project is Rs. 250 crore. Further, all hydro projects involving rivers
flowing through more than one State require CEA clearance. By
implication, this means that all the hydro projects irrespective of
capacity cost would need CEA node for execution. The Committee
had further observed that power project costing more than Rs. 100.00
crore needs clearance from Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs
(CCEA). In order to step up the utilization of funds, the Ministry of
Power had suggested that the existing procedures for obtaining
approval of projects need to be streamlined. The Ministry of Finance
had then responded that enhanced delegation had been permitted to
various Central Ministries including Power as recently as February,
2002. The Ministry of Finance had also stated that they were open
to any measure, which lead to faster improvement of power projects
as well as better utilization of funds allocated to power sector. Taking
note of the proposal of the Ministry of Power to enhance the
delegation of powers for implementation of power projects for the
consideration of the cabinet, the Committee find that the present
ceiling prescribed for CCEA approval is too meager. The Committee,
therefore, reiterate their earlier recommendation for enhance
delegation of powers to the Ministry and its PSUs. The Committee
also feel that there is a need for through analysis of the reasons for
delay which can be related to environment/forests, land acquisition,
law and order problems, tying up of financial resources, selling and
power purchase agreements, etc. At the same time, the Committee
favours the suggestion of the Ministry of Power regarding creation
of Power investment Commission for all projects in power sector on
the lines of Telecom Commission or the National Highway Authority
of India (NHAI) whereby PIB/CCEA clearance can be obtained for
5 years plan target irrespective of taking clearance for individual
projects. The Committee desire that the Ministry of Power should
immediately take up this matter with the Government at appropriate
level and apprise the Committee of the resultant outcome.

2.22 The Committee observe that capacity addition programme
of the Government during 9th Plan was no better than 8th Plan
achievements. Against a target capacity addition of 40245.2 MW set
for the 9th Plan, the actuals were only 19015 MW. The Committee
note that both Central and Private sectors have lagged behind the
targets set during 9th Plan in both thermal and hydel sectors. As
against the targets set for 7574 MW for Central Sector (Thermal),
achievement were only 3084 MW and the actuals were only 540 MW
for hydro power against the targets of 3455 MW. Similarly, Private
sector achieved capacity addition of 4975 MW of thermal power and
86 MW of hydro power generation against the targeted 17038.5 MW
and 550 MW of thermal and hydro power respectively. The
Committee, therefore, have come to an irresistible conclusion that
over-optimistic and unachievable targets are set by the Government
which have never come close to achievement during the last 2 Plan
periods. In spite of Committee’s earlier recommendations to project
realistic and achievable targets, the matter has not been seriously
considered. The hydel Sector has failed to materialize its targets,
consequently leading to adverse hydel thermal mix. Over-dependence
and a total reliance on private sector have failed to show any positive
result so far. It is in this context, the Committee reiterate their earlier
recommendation that it may not be desirable for the Government to

20
diminish their role or withdraw themselves from the power sector
lest private sector should fail again (29th Report of 13th Lok Sabha).
The Committee are of the opinion that power sector should be
rejuvenated and restructured. There is a need to extend adequate
Budgetary support to hydel sector, so that optimal 40 : 60 hydel-
thermal ratio mix be attained. The Planning Commission estimated
a feasible capacity addition of 47,000 MW during the 10th Plan.
Considering the 8th & 9th Plans performance, the Committee observe
that this target seems to be difficult to achieve. The Committee’s
close scrutiny has revealed that lack of investment decision in thermal
PSUs, delay in receipt of foreign assistance, submission of DPRs,
are some of the reasons under Central Thermal Sector, for projects
being slipped from 9th Plan. The projects under private sector slipped
on account of failure to achieve Financial Closure, litigation etc.
Funds constraints, land acquisition/R&R problems, adverse law &
order, contractual problems were some of the reasons attributed for
slippage of hydel Projects. A close look at these reasons indicate
that these are not the new reasons and it was precisely because of
these reasons the targets could not be achieved during the 8th Plan.
But, the Government did not take any corrective action to check
those reasons which resulted in failure of 9th Plan. The Committee,
therefore, reiterate their earlier recommendation that only achievable
and realistic targets with firm details of the source of funding for
capacity generation programme.  The Committee desire that
somewhere accountability should be fixed for projecting unrealistic
targets and failure to achieve the targets fixed. The Committee urge
that the Government should, at least now, ensure that the projected
10th Plan targets are achieved. The Committee would, therefore, like
to be apprised of the follow-up corrective action taken by the
Government.
C.  Energy Conservation
2.23 Energy conservation has emerged as one of the central issue
in national economic agenda in recent years. A potential of at least
25 percent reduction of energy consumption from the present level is
possible in the different sectors, without forgoing any of the end-use
benefits of energy. The individual and the society stand to gain from
conservation and improved energy efficiency, both in terms of money
saved by reducing energy costs in the short run, as well as reducing
investment needs for energy production in the long run. Energy
conservation also reduces or avoids the tremendous social and
environmental costs resulting from in energy generation and wasteful

21
consumption, such as emissions of carbon dioxide (CO 2) and other
pollutants and depletion of scarce resources and damage to the
environment. Despite the relatively low per capita energy use in India,
there is a need to increase energy availability to meet basic needs and
developmental goals. However, the high level of energy intensity in
some of the sectors is also a matter of concern. Hence, conservation
has to go hand in hand with generation efficiency. A systematic
understanding of energy consumption patterns is needed in each sector,
and a strategy has to be evolved to supply energy efficiently and
curtail wasteful consumption.
2.24 With the primary objective of reducing energy intensity of the
Indian Economy the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) was established
under the provisions of the Energy Conservation Act, 2001 w.e. 1st
March, 2002. The Ministry of Power has released one time corpus

2002-03. BEE has been authorized to invest the same in such a way to
earn the best return. The corpus fund was released to BE has been

The corpus fund was released to BEE during January 2003, which on
the advise of executive Committee of Bureau and Governing Council

Annually they are earning about Rs. 4 to 4.5 crore from the investment

2. PROGRESS/ACHIEVEMENTS MADE IN THE IMPLEMENTATION
OF THE ENERGY CONSERVATION ACT, 2001 AND ACTION PLAN
OF BEE
Majority of the project/scheme implemented by the Bureau during
its last two years of its establishments have been mainly on the setting
up of the institutional mechanism in order to facilitate the various
mandatory and voluntary provisions of the EC Act. The major
provisions of the EC Act, 2001 relate to the following areas and the
progress achieved in each area is given below:
(a) Designated Consumers
(i) The designated consumers have to appoint or designate
certified energy managers. For this purpose a national level
Certification Examination has been conducted on 22-23rd
May, 2004 in 23 centers spread all over the country. In total
2840 candidates registered for the Certification examination
and about 82% appeared in the examination. The programme
is self sustaining and Bureau has generated the revenue of
Rs. 347 lakhs. A very high rating of 91% (excellent and
very good) was given by the candidates for the overall
process of certification, quality of course material,
examination administration and its overall usefulness in
improving energy efficiency in the industrial and commercial
sectors.
(ii) The designated consumers have to get the energy audit
conducted by accredited energy auditors. 62 energy auditing
agencies have been short-listed after detailed evaluation of
their institutional and energy auditing capabilities.
(iii) To standardize the process of conduct of energy audit,
energy performance assessment codes for 7 technologies/
equipments have been prepared.
(iv) Specific energy consumption norms are to be met by the
designated consumers. As a pilot project, cement and pulp
& paper sectors have been selected for establishment of the
norms, which are to be ready by March 2005.
(v) To support designated consumers on information exchange
on best practices and undertaking of voluntary energy saving
targets, an Indian Industry Programme for energy
Conservation (IIPEC) has been launched. Eight sectoral Task

26
forces for cement, pulp & paper, textile, fertilizer, chlor-alkali,
aluminium, petro-chemical and refinery sectors have been
formed. Voluntary target of energy saving worth Rs. 400
crore have been committed by participating industries of
the above voluntary programme. Bureau has initiated the
process of collection of feed back on the achieved savings
by the Task Force members.
(vi) Two interactive Websites (www.bee-india.com&www.
energymanagertraining.com) to support industry on energy
conservation initiatives, have been made operational.
(b) Standards & Labeling Programme
(i) Technical parameters for energy labelling have been
developed for 5 products—Agricultural pump sets, Motors,
Fluorescent tube lights, Distribution transformers, Household
Refrigerator and Air conditioners have been taken up for
labeling.
(ii) Refrigerator testing-training imparted to engineers from
manufacturers and individual test laboratories.
(iii) Proficiency testing to insure accuracy of testing between labs
conducted for refrigerator test labs.
(iv) Consumer and market research for energy labels completed.
(c) Energy Efficiency in Buildings
(i) Energy audit studies completed in 9 government buildings

energy conservation scheme be held-up due to lack of funds. The

in this regard.

Plan include Indian Industry Programme for energy conservation,
demand side management, standard labelling programme, energy

research programme, school education, etc. The Committee further
observe that BEE has already taken various steps such as energy
audit in Central Government buildings, testing facilities for standard
and labelling guidelines for building codes, pilot project for school

generation (460 MW) against the investment on energy conservation

The Committee note that the Government have not furnished the
recurring benefits of the investments made in various industries as
the proportion of investments did not indicate the desired monetary
gains by the industry. In this context, the Committee would like to
be apprised of the recurring benefits which should accrue to the
industries on account of one time investments on energy conservation
devices.
2.36 The Committee feel that conservation and efficient use of
energy should be treated as one of the major thrust areas to bridge
the gap between the demand and supply of power. Although,
measures to promote conservation of energy have been taken, the
Committee are unhappy to note that energy audit in distribution

32
systems in Kerala, West Bengal which were targeted to be completed
in 1999-2000 by the Rural Electrification Corporation (REC) were
delayed and completed only in 2000-01. The Committee are further
dismayed to note that 3000 Amorphous Core Transformers which
were to be introduced in the States of Andhra Pradesh, Punjab,
Karnataka, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan
by REC by 1999-2000, were delayed and the scheme was completed
in 2003-04. The Committee observe similar fate of other schemes
implemented by agencies like the Punjab State Electricity Board,
HVPNL, TERI, etc. The Committee also observe that only one energy
conservation activity each in the year 2002-03 and 2003-04 was
completed by agencies other than BEE. The Committee are
constrained to note that although the Government on the one hand
are claiming high that a large number of schemes/activities have
been initiated to promote the energy efficiency and savings have
accrued, it seems that the Government have failed to enthuse
conservation and energy efficiency agencies for undertaking such
schemes. The Committee, therefore, reiterate their earlier
recommendation that there is a greater need to bring about public
awareness regarding energy efficiency measures of the Government
and the Government should set the targets to be achieved for energy
savings during a particular year. The Committee desire that short-
term as well as long-term action plans be formulated and the
Committee be apprised of the action taken by the Government in
this regard.
2.37 The Committee are unhappy to know that the Bureau of
Energy Efficiency (BEE) is still in the process of establishing
institutional mechanism to facilitate the implementation of the Energy
Conservation Act and therefore the activity of reviewing the energy
conservation equipment for 100% depreciation and other schemes
are being proposed to be taken up in the current financial year. The
Committee, therefore, recommend that the Government should take
immediate action for fiscal incentives to encourage faster penetration
of energy efficient technologies. The Committee stress that all these
issues be decided immediately and the Committee should be apprised
of the action taken in this regard within 3 months. The Committee
also feel that there is need for wider publicity to the various
provisions of the Energy Conservation Act which are likely to have
a direct bearing on ordinary consumers so that they are not caught
unaware when the Act is enforced.

D. Renovation & Modernisation (R&M)
Thermal Power Stations
2.38 Renovation & Modernisation (R&M) and Life Extension (LE)
of the existing old power stations has been recognised as one of the
most cost effective options to achieve additional generation by virtue
of the short gestation period and low cost. In addition to generation
improvement, other benefits such as life extension, improvement in
efficiency, availability, safety and environmental conditions are also
achieved through R&M and LE Programme. Keeping this in view, the
Government of India launched a Centrally sponsored scheme for R&M
of 34 nos. of Thermal power stations in the country under Phase-I
programme. Government of India sanctioned a Central Loan Assistance
(CLA) of Rs. 500 crore. The programme was completed in the year
1992 and an additional generation of about 10,000 MU/annum was
achieved against a target of 7000 MU/annum.
2.39 The Committee have been informed that encouraged with the
benefits achieved from the Phase-I programme during the 7th Plan,
the Phase-II programme for R&M of 44 nos. of thermal power stations
was taken up in the year 1990-91 for the 8th Plan at an estimated cost
of Rs. 2383 crore. Power Finance Corporation (PFC) was assigned to
provide loan assistance to the State Electricity Boards for R&M works.
All the schemes were identified by the Roving teams comprising of
engineers from CEA, BHEL and utilities. According to the Ministry of
Power, this programme could not progress as per schedule mainly
due to non availability of timely loan assistance and the weak financial
conditions of the SEBs/Utilities. By the end of 8th Plan i.e. upto March
1997, about 50% of the works could be completed on all India basis
and an expenditure of Rs. 862 crore was incurred. After partial
completion of the works, an additional generation of 500 MU/year
has been achieved. Also, the Life Extension works on 4 units (300
MW) of Neyveli Thermal Power Station were completed.
